title: Mouth of Truth (Bocca della Verità)
address: Piazza della Bocca della Verità, 18, 00186 Rome
scene_description: Joe Bradley pretends to lose his hand in the Mouth of Truth — Gregory Peck's improvised prank drawing a genuine shriek from Audrey Hepburn that William Wyler kept in the film. It's the moment the princess truly becomes a girl on holiday, and one of the most perfectly unguarded seconds ever captured on screen.
fun_fact: The Bocca della Verità is an ancient Roman marble mask, possibly a drain cover from the 1st century AD. Medieval legend held that it would bite off the hand of liars. Gregory Peck's decision to pull his hand into his sleeve and scream was unscripted — Audrey Hepburn's terrified reaction is completely real. Wyler loved it so much he built the entire scene around the joke.
then_and_now: The Mouth of Truth is in the portico of the Basilica of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. There's often a queue for photos — put your hand in, tell a lie, and channel your inner Audrey Hepburn. Free entry, but donations to the church are appreciated.

fun_fact: Piazza Navona was built on the site of the Stadium of Domitian (1st century AD), and its distinctive elongated shape traces the ancient racetrack. The Fountain of the Four Rivers by Bernini (1651) is one of Rome's greatest Baroque masterpieces. Paolo Sorrentino shot The Great Beauty here at 5 AM to capture the piazza empty — the only hour when Rome's most tourist-packed square belongs to the Romans.
then_and_now: One of Rome's most beautiful squares, ringed by cafés, artists, and street performers. Come at dawn like Jep — you'll have Bernini's fountains almost to yourself. Or come at night when the Baroque façades are lit and the piazza feels exactly like a film set.

title: Gallier Hall

scene_description: The imposing Greek Revival columns of Gallier Hall served as the exterior of the Théâtre des Vampires — where Lestat's theatrical coven performed their deadly masquerade for unsuspecting mortals.
fun_fact: Gallier Hall was New Orleans' City Hall from 1853 to 1958. For the film, the production dressed its neoclassical façade with elaborate theatrical banners and gas lamps to transform it into the vampires' playhouse.

title: Ursuline Convent
scene_description: The oldest building in the Mississippi Valley — its weathered brick walls and shuttered windows provided the perfect Gothic atmosphere for the vampire covens' earliest New Orleans scenes.
fun_fact: Completed in 1752, the Ursuline Convent survived the great fires of 1788 and 1794. It's the oldest surviving French colonial building in the United States. The film crew reportedly found the atmosphere so authentically eerie they barely had to dress the set.
then_and_now: The convent is now part of the Archdiocese archives. Visitors can tour the garden and chapel — no vampires in residence, though the creaking floorboards might suggest otherwise.

title: Beauregard-Keyes House
scene_description: The opulent interiors of this 1826 French Quarter mansion doubled as the vampire townhouse — where Louis first encounters Lestat's world of velvet curtains, candlelit salons, and the seductive horror of immortality.
fun_fact: Built as a residence for a wealthy auctioneer, the house later belonged to Confederate General P.G.T. Beauregard and then to novelist Frances Parkinson Keyes. The film used its grand ballroom and courtyard extensively for the vampire household scenes.
then_and_now: Open as a museum daily. The garden alone is worth the visit — one of the French Quarter's best-kept secrets, and instantly recognizable from the film.

title: Hermann-Grima House
address: 820 St Louis St, New Orleans, LA 70112
scene_description: The meticulously preserved 1831 Federal-style mansion — with its original courtyard kitchen and slave quarters — provided the period-authentic backdrop for the mortal world the vampires moved through so elegantly.
fun_fact: Hermann-Grima is one of the few French Quarter homes with its original outbuildings intact, including the only surviving open-hearth kitchen and stable in the Quarter. The film crew marveled at how little they needed to alter — the 19th century was already perfectly preserved.
then_and_now: A fascinating house museum with period cooking demonstrations in the original kitchen. The courtyard is a peaceful retreat from Bourbon Street's chaos — just around the corner but a world away.

title: Masonic Cemetery

scene_description: New Orleans' cities of the dead — above-ground tombs rising from the mist — made the perfect hunting ground for vampires who understood that in this city, the line between the living and the dead was always negotiable.
fun_fact: New Orleans cemeteries use above-ground tombs because the high water table would literally push buried coffins back to the surface. The Masonic Cemetery is one of the largest, with elaborate marble mausoleums that read like a who's who of 19th-century New Orleans society.
then_and_now: Guided cemetery tours run daily. Go with a knowledgeable guide — the stories behind the tombs are as rich as the architecture, and some of the Masonic symbolism is genuinely mysterious.
